clue.text: Clever person in college once getting most of a subject

parts.note: a poly, short for polytechnic, was a type of British college before 1992

indicators.note: most of says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: maths is a school subject

explanation.surface: A clever former polytechnic student who managed to learn most of a subject.
explanation.walkthrough: 'most of' drops the last letter of MATHS, leaving MATH. Polytechnics were British colleges that became universities in 1992.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone learned across many fields is a classic example of a clever person.

clue.text: Make susceptible drunk sip red with model

indicators.note: drunk suggests the letters are reeling about in a new order

parts.note: to pose is what a model does

explanation.surface: Getting someone tipsy on red wine while they model, to make them more pliable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' scrambles SIP RED into PREDIS.
explanation.definitionFit: To incline someone towards something in advance makes them susceptible to it.

clue.text: Fixing collar and evening dress, primarily before getting regional tie?

indicators.note: fixing suggests putting the letters into a new, sorted arrangement
primarily picks out the first letter of each of the two words

parts.note: by means before, as in by noon

explanation.surface: Adjusting a collar and evening dress before attending a regional event in a tie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fixing' is the anagram signal and 'primarily' takes initials. A local derby is a football match between two neighbouring teams; 'tie' in British sport means a match.
explanation.definitionFit: A match between nearby rivals is a fixture, or tie, between teams of one region.

clue.text: Present behind wrapping paper ultimately for Charlie

indicators.note: wrapping says the first piece goes around the second

parts.note: to moon is to show one's bare backside, presenting one's behind

indicators.note: ultimately picks out the last letter of the word paper

explanation.surface: A present for Charlie sits behind its wrapping paper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrapping' puts R, the last letter of 'paper', inside MOON. 'Charlie' is British slang for a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a charlie is a fool or idiot, someone stupid.

clue.text: Charge after sweeping road

indicators.note: after places the piece for charge following the other piece

parts.note: a sweeping change is a thorough one
a fare is the charge for a journey

explanation.surface: A fee charged after the road has been swept.
explanation.definitionFit: A main street or highway open to traffic is a road.

clue.text: Sweet FA, having turned 19 almost

indicators.note: having turned says the two letters of FA are read in reverse order
almost says the word loses its final letter

parts.note: 19 is the answer to 19 across, meaning brief or curt

explanation.surface: 'Sweet FA' is British slang for nothing at all, paired with a cross-reference to another clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet FA' reads as one phrase meaning 'nothing', but Sweet is the definition. 'almost' cuts the last letter from TERSE. In Britain, afters is an informal word for dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: A sweet is the dessert course, which British speakers casually call afters.

clue.text: Competitors before match experiment in practice

indicators.note: before places the piece for competitors ahead of the other

parts.note: the field is all the competitors in a race or contest
a test is a test match, an international cricket game

explanation.surface: Competitors warming up with practice before a match.
explanation.definitionFit: A trial carried out in real working conditions is an experiment done in practice.

clue.text: Polish detective in film

indicators.note: in says one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: E.T. is Spielberg's film about an extraterrestrial
DI stands for Detective Inspector

explanation.surface: A Polish detective appearing in a film.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Polish' looks like a nationality; read with a small p it means to refine text.
explanation.definitionFit: To polish a piece of writing is to revise and improve it.

clue.text: Kind men feeding good person

indicators.note: feeding says one piece goes into the other

parts.note: ST, for saint, is a good person
OR, other ranks, means the ordinary men of the army

explanation.surface: Kindly men feeding a good person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' looks like an adjective meaning generous, but here it is the noun meaning type.
explanation.definitionFit: A kind is a type or variety, the same as a category.

clue.text: Mark tucking into eggs, initially came to one with shell

indicators.note: tucking into says one piece is slipped inside the other
initially picks out the first letter of the word eggs

parts.note: came to, as in got to a place, means got
a scar is a mark left on the skin

explanation.surface: Someone tucking into eggs, then moving on to a snail course at dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tucking into' sends the mark between the initial of eggs and the rest; 'initially' takes only the first letter of 'eggs'.
explanation.definitionFit: A snail eaten as a French delicacy is a creature that carries a shell on its back.

clue.text: Thickness of hose from end — fire's beginning to go out

indicators.note: out signals that the letters gathered here are thrown into disorder
beginning to go says the word's first letter is dropped

parts.note: fire's is read as fire is, and the word fire is the piece used

explanation.surface: Something about stockings and a fire that is starting to go out at one end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beginning to go' drops the first letter, leaving IRE, and 'out' scrambles the result with the other word. 'go out' looks like one phrase but splits between two jobs.
explanation.definitionFit: A denier is the unit measuring the fineness of yarn, used to grade how sheer tights and stockings are.

clue.text: Awkward bra, anger miss with fumbling

indicators.note: fumbling suggests clumsy handling that leaves the letters jumbled

explanation.surface: A clumsy fumble with a bra, much to a young woman's annoyance.
explanation.definitionFit: An awkward situation is one that causes discomfort and shame.

clue.text: Clueless Tramp will notify editor

parts.note: the setter Tramp speaking of himself would say I'll
to notify someone is to inform them

explanation.surface: The setter cheerfully confesses he will tell his editor something, despite having no idea.
explanation.walkthrough: Tramp is the setter's pseudonym, so 'Tramp will' is the setter saying I'LL.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone clueless lacks knowledge, which is what being poorly briefed means.

clue.text: Kind of tea written on one board

indicators.note: written on, in a down clue, places the tea piece on top of the rest

parts.note: char is British slang for tea
one is the Roman numeral I
a table is a board, as in bed and board

explanation.surface: A type of tea whose name is written on a board.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind of' looks like a single phrase meaning type; 'Kind' alone is the definition, an adjective meaning generous.
explanation.definitionFit: A generous, benevolent person is kind.

clue.text: Way they might bring up food for Pilates class?

parts.note: ST, for street, is a way
people who retch are those who might bring up food

explanation.surface: A gym-goer's warning that Pilates students might be sick.
explanation.definitionFit: A Pilates class is full of people who stretch, so a whimsical name for them is those who stretch.

clue.text: Start to put on pair of smalls and hug

indicators.note: start to picks out the first letter of the word put

parts.note: RE means on, as in regarding or concerning
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels, so two of them give SS

explanation.surface: Pulling on a pair of underpants and then embracing someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smalls' is British slang for underwear, which steers the surface; here it is just two S's for 'small'.
explanation.definitionFit: To hug someone is to squeeze or clasp them close to you.

clue.text: A record's for playing around clubs?

definitions.text: A record's for playing around clubs?

indicators.note: around says the scrambled letters go round the other piece
playing suggests the letters are played around with into a new order

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for clubs, the card suit

explanation.surface: A record kept while playing a round with golf clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for playing' scrambles A RECORD'S, which then goes 'around' C for clubs; the whole clue also describes a golfer's card.
explanation.definitionFit: A golfer's card records strokes for each hole while playing a round.

clue.text: Balls from iron in golf, hit stroke over middle of green

indicators.note: over says the piece for stroke comes after the centre of green

parts.note: G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet
to rap is to hit sharply

indicators.note: middle of picks out the centre letter of the word green

parts.note: a shot is a stroke in golf or tennis

explanation.surface: A golfer hits an iron shot over the middle of the green.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf words (iron, stroke, green) belong to the surface; 'iron' is part of the definition, as grapeshot was small iron balls fired from a cannon.
explanation.definitionFit: Grapeshot is cannon ammunition made of clusters of small metal balls.

clue.text: Low-pitched noise from this replacement dog

parts.note: a sub is a substitute or replacement player
a woofer, a creature that woofs, is a jocular word for a dog

explanation.surface: A substitute dog making a deep growling sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A loudspeaker built for bass frequencies is the source of low-pitched sound.

clue.text: Some after sex that's quick

indicators.note: Some says the answer is a run of letters hidden inside the words that follow

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: A cheeky line about something brief happening after lovemaking.
explanation.definitionFit: A curt, brief remark is quick, using few words.

clue.text: Boris Johnson is one in pieces, upset with court

indicators.note: upset says the letters of the two words are knocked over and rearranged

explanation.surface: A former Prime Minister in pieces, troubled by a court case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in pieces' also hints at the anagram, though 'pieces' itself is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Boris Johnson campaigned for Brexit, making him an example of someone hostile to the European Union.

clue.text: Space at front of border for plant

indicators.note: at front of places the space piece ahead of the other

parts.note: an em is a printer's space, as wide as the letter M
a border is a flower bed

explanation.surface: Leaving a gap at the front of a flower border for a plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plant' looks like a noun in the garden scene but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To plant something firmly in a surface is to fix it deep inside.

clue.text: Rabbits on film

definitions.meaning: to rabbit is British slang for to chatter on

explanation.surface: Rabbits appearing on film.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses fit: chattering at length, and the famous shark thriller.

clue.text: Woman is con artist

parts.note: to do someone is to swindle or con them
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: A woman unmasked as a con artist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'con artist' looks like one swindler, but each word gives its own piece; RA, Royal Academician, is a standard crossword artist.
explanation.definitionFit: Dora is a female first name, so it stands for a woman.

clue.text: With no scruples, nose goes over line

indicators.note: goes over says the word flips over, read backwards

parts.note: a wine's nose is its aroma

explanation.surface: Someone unscrupulous whose nose crosses a line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes over' turns AROMA backwards to give AMORA.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking any moral sense means having no scruples at all.

clue.text: Shortly go with male and attractive girl to house with land

indicators.note: shortly says the word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: zip means go, energy or vigour

indicators.note: to house says one piece holds the other inside it

parts.note: a babe is slang for an attractive young woman

explanation.surface: A man hurrying off with a pretty girl to set up home together on some land.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Shortly' trims the last letter; 'to house' puts the abbreviation for with inside the girl, so the pieces join in a different order from the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Zimbabwe is a country in southern Africa, and a country is a land.

clue.text: Drink shot with slices in

indicators.note: slices in says one piece cuts its way into the other

parts.note: a shy is a throw or attempt, a shot at something
and means with, joining two things

explanation.surface: A drink served as a shot with slices of lemon in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'slices in' sends the word for with into the throw. Shandy is beer mixed with lemonade, a British pub drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Shandy, beer mixed with lemonade, is a drink served in pubs.

clue.text: One beam, say, brought back to son's old property

parts.note: one is A, the indefinite article

indicators.note: brought back says the pieces are read in reverse order

parts.note: to beam a signal is to send it
say means for example, abbreviated EG
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A beam from an old house being returned to its owner's son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brought back' turns SENDEG backwards to give GEDNES.
explanation.definitionFit: Being elderly is the quality or property of old age.
